hydroponics: Monkey Blog · Home Growing Home EN PT Home growing · a manual in sixteen parts Hydroponics at Home Roots in water instead of earth, a pump that keeps them breathing, and a nutrient solution you mix in a bucket. This manual takes that idea the whole way: six systems, the chemistry, the build you can make from what a city throws away, twelve steps from seed to plate, and the failures that kill a crop in a week. Six systems City-waste builds Water chemistry Seed to plate Portugal calendar Sources I want a first bucket this weekend Sections 01, 02 and 06, then the dated first month. Forty euros, one afternoon. I want to build it from waste Section 03: what is safe to reuse, six builds, what never goes near a reservoir. Something is dying Section 11: symptoms, the diagnosis order, pests, and what each leaf pattern means. I want to know what to sow now Section 08 opens on the current month, with a full Portuguese year behind it. 01 What a plant actually needs A plant does not eat soil. Soil holds the roots still, keeps them damp, lets air reach them and slowly releases minerals. Do those four jobs another way and the soil becomes optional — not magic, just one supplier among several. job 1 Support Net pots, clay pebbles, rockwool cubes or a foam collar hold the stem upright. A heavy fruit needs a string or a stake, not the pot. job 2 Water The solution reaches the roots continuously or in cycles. What soil did by capillarity, here a pump, a wick or a falling film does. job 3 Oxygen Roots respire. Wet roots without air suffocate in days, which is why every system that works either moves the water or bubbles air through it. job 4 Minerals Nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, calcium, magnesium and the trace elements arrive dissolved and measured, instead of waiting to be released by soil life. The honest ledger Hydroponics is a tool for space, control and clean water — not an automatic claim to sustainability. The trade is specific, and it is worth knowing before you buy anything. What you gain 70–90 % less water than the same crop in open soil, because nothing drains away. No weeds, no soil-borne pests, no digging, no backache. Growth is faster when light and oxygen are right — often two or three weeks per cycle. The garden moves with you: indoors in November, balcony in April. You see the plant's food. EC and pH are a dashboard no soil grower gets. What you pay for it A pump or power failure is fatal within hours in warm weather — the roots have no reservoir of soil. Water chemistry becomes your job, and mistakes show up as leaf edges two weeks later. Energy: a controlled-environment study found lettuce yields 11× higher per area but 82× the energy per head, mostly lighting. Plastic, salts and meters are consumables; a system is a small appliance, not a closed loop. You buy the nutrients. Compost does not dissolve, and manure tea does not belong in a recirculating reservoir. The one-line version: hydroponics replaces soil with plumbing, and plumbing fails loudly. It is at its best where soil is impossible — a fourth-floor flat, a dark January, a balcony with 0.4 m² — and at its worst as a promise that it will save money. 02 Six systems, one ladder Six ways to keep roots wet and breathing. They are ordered by how much can go wrong, not by how impressive they look: start at the top and move down only when a plant — not boredom — gives you the reason. Start here: Kratky, or a wick No electricity, no timer, no noise. Lettuce, basil, rocket, pak choi. If this fails, the cause is temperature or light, and you learn it for €5. Then: one deep-water bucket Add an air pump and a 20 L reservoir and you can grow a tomato. The pump is the first thing that can break, and the first thing worth learning to hear. Then: drip or a channel A timer, emitters, a return line: this is where a home system starts to behave like a small machine and needs a weekly inspection, not a glance. Only if you must: aeroponics The fastest growth and the shortest grace period. A clogged nozzle kills a crop before lunch. Run it beside a bucket, never instead of one. Kratky DWC NFT Drip Aeroponics Wick best first system Kratky — passive, no pump, no electricity A jar, a net pot, nutrient solution. The roots drink, the level drops, an air gap forms and the upper roots breathe it. Nothing moves, nothing hums. Lettuce, basil, rocket, pak choi: one plant per 1–3 litre jar, 4–6 weeks. watch out Limits Water temperature decides everything: above 24 °C the solution runs out of oxygen and root rot starts. Not for tomatoes or anything that lives four months. Change the solution every two weeks; never top up to the brim once roots hang in the air gap. the workhorse Deep water culture — bucket, lid, air stone 10–20 litres in a bucket, an aquarium air pump with a stone, roots permanently submerged and constantly oxygenated. Fast growth, forgiving of a missed top-up, and the cheapest way to grow a real tomato plant indoors. watch out Details Keep the water at 18–22 °C — a black bucket in the sun will cook it; wrap it in foil or paint it white. One 3–5 W pump per two buckets is enough. If the pump stops for a day in summer, the plant may not survive. for many small plants Nutrient film technique — a shallow stream in a channel A pump lifts solution to one end of a tilted pipe; a 2–3 mm film runs past the roots and drains back into the tank. Excellent for 20 lettuce heads on a shelf, poor for fruit: the channel is too small for a big root ball. watch out Details A blocked channel starves a whole row in an hour. Slope 1–2 %, never more. Filter the return, and check flow daily in hot weather. for fruit Drip — a pot of pebbles, watered on a timer Each plant sits in clay pebbles; a small pump drips solution onto the pot three to six times a day and it drains back to the tank. The standard way to grow tomatoes, peppers, cucumbers, strawberries and herbs from one shared reservoir. watch out Details Emitters clog with nutrient salts — clean them monthly in warm water. Because the reservoir is shared, one sick plant spreads to all: inspect roots weekly. advanced Aeroponics — roots in air, misted Roots hang in a closed box; nozzles spray a fine mist every few minutes. The highest oxygen levels of any method and the fastest growth — and the least tolerant of failure: a clogged nozzle means dead roots in hours. watch out Details Needs a timer with seconds, a filter, and a spare pump. Do not start here. If you want the experiment, run it beside a DWC so one crop survives. simplest possible Wick — a cord does the pumping A cotton or nylon cord runs from a reservoir into a pot of pebbles or coco coir and pulls solution up by capillarity. Good for herbs, lettuce and a windowsill, and it cannot flood the roots. watch out Details Weak flow limits big plants, and the cord clogs with salts after a month or two — replace it. Coco coir buffers the pH and hides the water, so check the reservoir weekly rather than the surface. The same six, side by side Cost is for the first build in Portugal, late 2026; failure mode is what happens when the power goes out in July. System Moving parts Cost Best crop When it fails Choosing by what you want to eat Start from the plate, not from the catalogue What you want System Floor space Effort Salad and herbs for one person Kratky jars or wick 0.2 m² Minutes a week Lettuce every week NFT channel or DWC 0.5–1 m² Weekly top-up Tomatoes, peppers, cucumber DWC buckets or drip 1–2 m² Twice a week Strawberries Drip or wide NFT channels 0.5 m² Twice a week Microgreens Shallow tray, no system at all 0.1 m² Every 2 days 03 Build it from the city's waste Every reservoir in this manual can be bought new for forty euros, or found for nothing. A city produces exactly the containers a hydroponic garden needs — food-grade drums, bakery crates, pipes, shelving — and throws most of them away after one use. The skill is not finding them. It is knowing which ones are safe. Why reuse beats recycling. A kilo of new HDPE carries roughly 1.8–2 kg of CO₂e before it holds a drop of water; a 20-litre drum weighs about a kilo. Reusing it saves the material, the moulding energy and the €6 — while recycling it saves only part of the first. The EU's own hierarchy puts prevention and reuse above recycling, and the plastics strategy is built on that order. A garden that buys new plastic every season is not circular, whatever the bucket is made of. The rule that matters more than the number The little triangle tells you the polymer. It does not tell you what the container held, who made it, or what was added to it. History beats code: a #2 drum that carried screen wash is scrap, and a #5 tub that carried yoghurt is a seedling pot after one wash. Buy nothing that ever held a biocide, a solvent, a fuel, a paint or anything whose label you cannot read. The seven resin codes, as they apply to a reservoir — not to a bottle of water Code Polymer Where you find it For a reservoir Clean it like a vessel, not like a dish A used container carries two things you cannot see: the residue of what it held, and a biofilm that will feed algae and root rot. Five steps, forty minutes, once per container. Strip the label and the glue Warm water with a spoon of bicarbonate, or a little cooking oil on the adhesive. Solvents are not worth the risk on something that will hold plant food. Scrub, do not soak Hot water, washing-up liquid, a brush that reaches the corners. Rinse until the water runs clear and no foam remains. Never use a scouring pad on the inside of a reservoir: the scratches become a permanent home for biofilm. Sanitise with dilute bleach One part thin household bleach (about 5 %) to nine parts water, ten minutes of contact, then two full rinses. Three per cent hydrogen peroxide works too, at 3 ml per litre, with no rinse needed. Never mix bleach with an acid — including pH-down. Bleach plus acid releases chlorine gas. Dry it in the sun Ultraviolet light is free disinfectant. An hour upside down on a balcony does more than a second wash. Store dry, lid off, so it cannot grow a smell. Test the rinse water Fill with clean water, stir, read the EC. If it climbs above 0.1 mS/cm, something is still dissolving out of the plastic. Rinse again, or demote the container to holding pebbles. Five builds, from a bottle to a tote Each is a complete, working system. The dimensions are the ones that fit a windowsill or a balcony in a Portuguese flat; scale them, do not shrink them — a reservoir that is too small is the most common reason a build fails in August. build 1 · €0–3 · 20 minutes The 5-litre bottle Kratky One bottle, one net pot, one lettuce. The cheapest honest test of whether you enjoy this. A 5 L PET water bottle, label off, top cut at the shoulder A net pot that sits in the neck, or a plastic cup with holes Clay pebbles, or washed gravel A seedling in a rockwool cube or a plug Wrap the bottle in paper or paint it: clear plastic grows algae in a week. Fill with solution to about a third, EC 0.8, pH 5.8. Seat the plant so the cube's bottom just touches the liquid. Never top up to the brim. The air gap that forms as the level drops is what the upper roots breathe. One crop per bottle: PET softens in sun and holds smells. Refill once, then recycle it and start a new one. build 2 · €12 new, €0 found · one afternoon The 20-litre drum DWC The workhorse. Two lettuce, or one tomato, with an air stone and a lid you can cut. A 20 L HDPE drum: a food bucket from a bakery, or a jerry can from a car wash An aquarium air pump, 2–3 W, with stone and 1 m of tube Two 8 cm net pots and 3 L of clay pebbles A lid, or a piece of rigid foam board cut to size Cut two holes in the lid, 8 cm, spaced as far apart as the drum allows. Drill a 6 mm notch for the air tube at the rim, not through the lid's middle. Fill to 2 cm below the pots, start the pump, and check for bubbles before planting. Wrap the drum in an old rice sack: it keeps light out and heat down for nothing. Food buckets from bakeries held mayonnaise, olives or pickles — safe after the wash. A drum that held engine oil never becomes a reservoir, whatever you clean it with. build 3 · €15 new, €5 found · for 6–10 plants The gutter or crate NFT A length of gutter, a bakery crate with a liner, or a plastic cable tray: anything that holds a 2 mm film and slopes. 2 m of PVC or PP gutter, with two end caps A 10 L tank and a 5 W submersible pump Net pots, 5 cm, one per 20 cm A lid or black membrane to keep light off the film Set the channel on two bricks: 2 cm of fall over 2 m is 1 %, which is enough. Feed at the high end through a 4 mm tube; drain at the low end through a bulkhead or a drilled cap. Cut pot holes 20 cm apart and cover the rest of the channel with a lid. Run the pump continuously for lettuce; five minutes on, fifteen off for herbs. Old PVC gutters can contain lead stabilisers and are a poor choice for edible crops. Prefer new PP, or a food crate with a food-grade liner. build 4 · €20–40 found · a balcony or a yard The IBC tote, cut in half A 1000 L IBC that carried juice or syrup is the best free reservoir a city offers: food-grade HDPE, a steel cage, and a tap already fitted. One 1000 L IBC, food-grade, with its cage and pallet A saw, a file, and gloves A submersible pump and 13 mm hose Net pots and pebbles for the raft, or six pots for drip Cut it a third from the top: the shallow part becomes a raft bed, the deep part a reservoir. File every edge — a cut IBC is a blade. Wear gloves, not sandals. Drill an overflow 3 cm below the raft's rim and plumb it back to the reservoir. Float a foam board with 5 cm holes: lettuce and basil on top, water underneath. A full 1000 L tote weighs a tonne. Put it on a ground-floor terrace or over a load-bearing wall, never on a balcony slab without checking what it was designed for. build 5 · €0 · five minutes The wick tub, for herbs and a north window Two tubs stacked, one wick, no electricity. The one system that survives a fortnight away. A 1 L yoghurt tub with its lid, plus a second tub as the reservoir A strip of old cotton T-shirt, 3 cm wide and 20 cm long Coco coir or pebbles, and a herb seedling Cut a slot in the upper tub's base and thread the cotton through, 5 cm inside. Fill the lower tub with solution, set the upper tub inside so the wick dips. Plant into the coir, water once from above, and leave it. Replace the wick every two months: it clogs with salts and stops lifting water. Wicks suit basil, mint, parsley and lettuce. They cannot deliver enough water for a tomato in July. Where a city keeps its parts Ask once, in person, and most of these become a weekly supply. Nobody at a bakery is attached to the bucket the mayonnaise came in. Twelve sources, what to ask for, and the catch Source Ask for Becomes Catch Never in a reservoir, whatever the label says: Anything that held oil, fuel, antifreeze, screen wash, paint, solvent, pesticide or a cleaning product. Plastic absorbs; rinsing does not undo it. Black recycled plastic from electronics, for anything that touches solution. It is often e-waste derived and can carry flame retardants. Galvanised steel, copper, brass or zinc fittings in contact with the solution — zinc and copper are toxic to roots at surprisingly low levels. Old PVC pipe or vinyl hose for edible crops; historic lead stabilisers are the reason it is avoided in drinking-water plumbing. Treated, painted or unknown timber, and pallets stamped MB (methyl bromide). HT, heat-treated, is the one to take. Tyres, polystyrene fish boxes and anything that smells of its last contents after two washes. About microplastics, honestly. Every plastic reservoir sheds a little, and warm, slightly acidic nutrient solution is a mildly aggressive environment. Choose HDPE or PP over PET, keep the tank out of the sun, do not scrub the inside, and replace anything cracked or chalky. The World Health Organization found no evidence of harm from microplastics in drinking water at current levels, and your lettuce is not drinking it — but "no evidence of harm" is not the same as "no plastic", and a glass jar is still the better choice for a windowsill. 04 Water is the medium In soil, water is an ingredient. Here it is the room the roots live in, so its temperature, its hardness and what your municipality put in it all become part of the recipe. Four sources, in the order a city dweller should consider them. the best one Rain from your own roof Nearly zero EC, no chlorine, free. One millimetre of rain on one square metre of roof is one litre; forty square metres of roof in Lisbon collect about 25 000 litres a year, which is a hundred times what a small system drinks. the default Tap water Perfectly usable. Let it stand 12–24 hours for chlorine, or neutralise chloramine with 50 mg of ascorbic acid per 10 litres. Read its EC before you add anything: that number is your floor. the free bonus Condensate from an air conditioner A working split unit in a Portuguese summer produces litres a day at almost zero EC. Fine for topping up a reservoir; not for drinking, and not for an aeroponic mister, where the aerosol is inhaled. with a caveat Water from an aquarium Mild nutrients and living microbes — excellent for a wick pot or the soil garden, risky in a sterile recirculating system where you cannot see what is blooming. Never pour it into a shared reservoir. Catching rain without making a mess A downpipe, a first-flush diverter, a filter and an opaque tank with a mosquito screen. The first two litres off a dry roof carry bird droppings and dust — discard them. Keep the tank dark: light grows algae, and an algae tank costs you more in pH swings than the water saved. On a balcony, a 100–200 L barrel under a downpipe is enough for a small system and a few pots, and it weighs 200 kg when full, so put it over a wall, not over the neighbour. Hard water. If your tap starts above EC 0.6, part of the reading is calcium and magnesium you did not add. Use rain or filtered water, or subtract the tap reading from the target and feed the difference. Never chase EC 3.0 with water that already sits at 1.0 without watching the leaf tips for burn. Temperature is oxygen Warm water holds less oxygen, and roots burn through oxygen faster when it is warm. This is the single number that decides whether a passive system lives through August. Keep the solution under 24 °C, and treat 26 °C as an alarm. Oxygen saturation of fresh water at sea level, and what it means for roots Water °C O₂ saturation mg/L What happens 15 10.1 Comfortable. Lettuce grows without complaint. 20 9.1 The target range for most home systems. 24 8.4 The line. Add air, shade the tank, or both. 28 7.8 Warm, oxygen-poor, and where root rot begins. 30 7.6 Emergency: chill, shade, increase flow, or harvest early. Roots want at least 5 mg/L of dissolved oxygen, which is why an air stone is not optional in deep water culture. A frozen 1.5 L bottle dropped into the tank in the evening buys a hot afternoon; a white or foil-wrapped tank buys the whole summer; a pump that runs at night buys the margin between the two. 05 Nutrients and the only two numbers pH and EC. One says whether the food is available, the other says how much food is there. Two meters cost about €30 together, and they replace every guess in this manual. Target ranges by crop (mS/cm = EC; 1 mS/cm ≈ 500–700 ppm depending on the meter's scale) Crop pH EC mS/cm Days to harvest Litres / plant pH: the lock on the cupboard Most crops want pH 5.5–6.5. Below 5.5 calcium and magnesium lock up; above 6.5 iron does. Adjust downwards with phosphoric or citric acid, upwards with potassium bicarbonate — a few drops at a time, stirring between each, because the response is not linear. Then measure again 24 hours later: drift is normal, a jump of more than 0.5 in a day means too little water or too much plant. EC: the strength of the soup EC measures total dissolved salts, not a nutrient. It cannot tell nitrogen from sodium. That is why you measure it
i3Hero: ↶ Home Field Manual I3H-1 · a WM that obeys, one line at a time i3 Desktop — From Nothing to Hero The tiling window manager that fits in one config file and one head. This page is the road from a bare X session to a desk that is yours: the config file, the keys, workspaces, the bar, icons that actually render, the extra software that glues a desktop together, and a complete annotated fancy config — every value explained by the line that sets it. config · workspaces · glyphs · rofi · picom vanilla JS · CSS3 · no dependencies every value reversible, one line at a time 01 From nothing i3 is a tiling window manager for X11, created by Michael Stapelberg and friends, with two rare virtues among WMs: it is complete without a desktop environment , and it is configured entirely in one text file that you can read, version and print. Nothing is hidden behind a GUI settings tool — that is not a limitation, it is the whole culture. Tiling by default: windows share the screen instead of covering each other. The mouse survives for exactly two jobs — resizing and clicking sometimes. Keyboard-driven by contract: $mod (usually Super ) plus a letter does everything. Stable where it matters: the IPC protocol and the config language have stayed compatible for over a decade; configs from 2012 still work in 2026. Siblings of the family: i3blocks , i3lock , i3status , and the Wayland rewrite sway (same config language). $ apt install i3 i3lock i3status # or pkg / dnf / pacman equivalents $ echo "exec i3" > ~/.xinitrc $ startx # or pick i3 at your display manager's login First launch runs i3-config-wizard : it writes a starter config and asks one question that matters for the rest of your life — your Super / Alt preference for $mod , plus how you want Win -key alternatives laid out. Choose Super : Alt belongs to the applications Emacs, Firefox and everything in between. Note: the wizard's output is just a normal config file. Everything it wrote can be re-edited by hand from now on, and this page assumes ~/.config/i3/config (or ~/.i3/config , whose existence it still honours as a fallback). 02 The configuration file One file: ~/.config/i3/config . Plain text, one directive per line, # for comments. There are no plugins, no modules, no scripts inside — which is why you never fear a typo breaking half of your desktop at once. Directive Means set $mod Mod4 Name a key once, use it everywhere ( Mod4 = Super , Mod1 = Alt ). bindsym Bind one key combo to an action or a command ( bind gives named modes with fallbacks). exec / exec_always Run a program at startup; exec_always also reruns on i3 restart . assign / for_window Send new windows to workspaces / apply rules to matching windows (criteria in [brackets] ). bar { } The block that defines the whole bar (position, status command, colours, tray). set_from_resource Read a value from X resources before falling back to a literal (nice for theming). # ~/.config/i3/config — smallest honest start (numbers in comments explain lines) set $mod Mod4 # 01: Super is the leader key set $term xterm # 02: one terminal variable, used everywhere below bindsym $mod+Return exec $term # 03 bindsym $mod+Shift+q kill # 04 bindsym $mod+h split h # 05 bindsym $mod+v split v # 06 bindsym $mod+j focus down # 07 bindsym $mod+k focus up # 08 bindsym $mod+Shift+j move down # 09 bindsym $mod+Shift+k move up # 10 bindsym $mod+1 workspace 1 # 11: one line per workspace bindsym $mod+2 workspace 2 bindsym $mod+Shift+c reload # 12: re-read the config, keep windows bindsym $mod+Shift+r restart # 13: restart i3 entirely bindsym $mod+Shift+e exec "i3-nagbar -t warning -m 'Exit i3?' -B 'Yes' 'i3-msg exit'" The two reload commands are different and worth knowing early: reload re-reads the config into the running session; restart replaces the WM process itself — the reason an X restart is rarely needed to fix WM problems. Note: i3-msg is the command-line twin of the keys: run i3-msg workspace 3 from a shell to switch workspaces, i3-msg 'resize grow width 40 px' to poke the layout from scripts or i3-nagbar . i3 --moreversion also tells you at a glance if you broke something with the config when i3 refuses a reload. 03 Keys first, mouse optional The key grammar is one verb family: focus , move , workspace , layout , resize , mark . Learn it once and it survives any monitor arrangement: Chord Action The sentence it writes $mod+d exec dmenu_run A launcher appears; type to run anything installed. $mod+w / $mod+s / $mod+e layout tabbed / stacking / toggle split Each container cycles between the three layouts. $mod+f / $mod+Shift+space fullscreen toggle / floating toggle Escape hatches when a tiling assumption breaks. $mod+space focus mode_toggle Move focus between tiled and floating windows. $mod+r resize (mode) Enter the built-in resize arrows mode; same keys again to leave. $mod+Shift+s sticky toggle sticky flag Floating window follows you across workspaces. $mod+a / $mod+Shift+a focus parent / focus child Walk the container tree instead of hashtables of corners. Note: bindsym binds the keysym; bindcode binds keycodes and survives layout switches on non-English keyboards. If your national characters break bindsym bindings, switch those specific binds to bindcode with xev to find the code. 04 Workspaces and layout Workspaces are i3's answer to virtual desktops: ten of them by default, bound to $mod+1..10 and named whatever you like (icons in section 07 use names, not numbers): set $ws1 "1: term" set $ws2 "2: web" set $ws10 "10: mail" bindsym $mod+1 workspace $ws1 bindsym $mod+2 workspace $ws2 bindsym $mod+Shift+2 move container to workspace $ws2 Layout is a tree. Each workspace holds containers ; each container splits horizontally/vertically, or switches to tabbed/stacking. The tree is why: $mod+e (toggle split) flips the last container's split direction — the "swap two windows' arrangement" trick. $mod+a then $mod+v / $mod+h changes where the next window appears : focus parent first, then split — the honest way to do “open my editor below my browser inside workspace 2”. $mod+Shift+1..10 moves a window to another workspace, and with $mod+Shift+space first it can float instead. # window rules on the tree (for_window + criteria) for_window [class="^xfce4-notes"] floating enable assign [class="^ Firefox$"] $ws2 assign [class="^thunderbird\ "] $ws10 Note: find the exact class / title strings with xprop (click the window): WM_CLASS(STRING) is what criteria use. Guess never; everyone who guesses ends up with rules that match the wrong window. 05 Starting things automatically i3 has one startup mechanism and no autostart daemon folklore: /etc/i3/config exec lines (yours, in ~/.config/i3/config ). exec --no-startup-id nm-applet # network tray applet exec --no-startup-id picom -b # compositor, daemon mode (section 10) exec --no-startup-id dunst # notifications server exec_always --no-startup-id feh --bg-scale ~/Pictures/wall.jpg exec --no-startup-id xss-lock --transfer-sleep-lock --i3lock --nofork Two honesty points: --no-startup-id stops i3 from grabbing focus for the started window — desktops lose their minds less when this flag is used. That is all of it. No ~/.config/autostart , no XFCE daemons, no systemd user units required here. If a program refuses to start this way (an updater that insists) put it in your ~/.xprofile file instead; but the config is where desk-startup belongs. Note: the xss-lock line is the sane way to wire i3lock to suspend: the screen locks itself before the laptop sleeps, so the password prompt is waiting when the lid opens. 06 The bar, without tears i3's built-in bar is driven by the bar { } block in the config and a status command that prints one line of text: i3status by default, i3blocks or polybar when you outgrow it. bar { position top status_command i3status -c ~/.config/i3/i3status.conf tray_output primary font pango:JetBrainsMono Nerd Font 10 separator_symbol " | " colors { background #0b110d statusline #eef4f0 separator #9aaf9e focused_workspace #9fe870 #1f3a24 #0b110d active_workspace #4d6b52 #16241a #9aaf9e inactive_workspace #16241a #0b110d #5f7a63 urgent_workspace #ff9d5c #3a241f #0b110d } } And a minimal ~/.config/i3/i3status.conf to feed it: general { interval = 5 colors = true } order += "wireless _first_" order += "ethernet _first_" order += "battery all" order += "load" order += "time" wireless _first_ { format_up = "%quality %essid" format_down = "" } ethernet _first_ { format_up = "%ip" format_down = "" } battery all { format = "%status %percentage %remaining" } time { format = "%H:%M:%S" } Note: i3blocks swaps the INI above for a set of little scripts named by block; anything that can print a line to stdout can be a block. That model, plus glyph fonts (next section), is where a laptop bar stops being a battery line and starts being a dashboard. 07 Icons that render i3 has no icon system of its own — the only “icons” on an i3 desk are glyphs in a font , used in three places: workspace names, status blocks, and per-window titles ( for_window rules). The one prerequisite is a font that actually contains the glyphs: $ apt install fonts-noto fonts-jetbrains-mono fonts-nerd-fonts-meta # or the classic trinity: fonts-font-awesome, ttf-nerd-fonts-symbols, fonts-emojione $ fc-list | grep -i "nerd\|awesome" # confirm the family name you will type in configs Then the font name (exact, from fc-list ) becomes the config currency: # everywhere in the WM — the exact family name from fc-list, not a guess: font pango:JetBrainsMono Nerd Font 10 # workspace names carry their glyphs directly (Unicode code points): set $ws1 "1: term" set $ws2 "2: " bindsym $mod+1 workspace $ws1 # and per-app window titles can too: for_window [class="Firefox"] title_format "2: %title" Some of the most useful code points, from a Nerd Font / Font Awesome at their conventional places (your fc-list family decides how they look, not the config):  house  laptop  battery  wifi  volume  code  globe  mail  tv  wrench Note: both i3status and i3blocks print these glyphs straight out of shell scripts — the block script's stdout is the bar. UTF-8 in, bar out; no plugin layer, no daemon to restart (well: killall -USR1 i3blocks if you swap scripts live, or plain restart which everyone does instead). Warn: if a glyph shows as a box, the family name in font pango:... does not match fc-list exactly — case, hyphen and last word all count ( Nerd Font , not NerdFonts ; Font Awesome 6 Free , not FontAwesome6 ). The fix is always in one place: the font line. 08 Extra software that glues the desk An i3 install is deliberately naked. The extras below are what turn it from a WM into a desk, with the role each one plays in one sentence: Tool Fills One-line install shape rofi dmenu's GTK-styled cousin: launcher, window switcher and much more with themes bindsym $mod+d exec rofi -show drun picom Compositor: shadows, transparency, vsync, no screen tearing exec --no-startup-id picom -b -c dunst Notification daemon for real (dbus) notifications exec --no-startup-id dunst feh / nitrogen Wallpaper setter (feh is the scripted one) exec_always --no-startup-id feh --bg-fill ~/w.png i3lock Screen lock, with colour or blur background bindsym $mod+Shift+x exec i3lock -c 000000 maim / scrot Screenshots (selection / whole screen) bindsym Print exec maim -s ~/shot.png network-manager-applet Wifi/network in the tray + password prompts exec --no-startup-id nm-applet pavucontrol Per-app volume when hotkeys are not enough bindsym $mod+F11 exec pavucontrol autorandr Remembers monitor layouts per physical arrangement exec --no-startup-id autorandr --change xss-lock Ties lock/suspend together exec --no-startup-id xss-lock -- i3lock -c 000000 The glue lines most desks end up wanting, exactly as written: # volume keys, PulseAudio flavour (swap pactl for amixer on pure ALSA boxes) bindsym XF86AudioRaiseVolume exec --no-startup-id pactl set-sink-volume @DEFAULT_SINK@ +5% bindsym XF86AudioLowerVolume exec --no-startup-id pactl set-sink-volume @DEFAULT_SINK@ -5% bindsym XF86AudioMute exec --no-startup-id pactl set-sink-mute @DEFAULT_SINK@ toggle # brightness (libinput-backed laptops use the sysfs path; check `ls /sys/class/backlight/`) bindsym XF86MonBrightnessUp exec --no-startup-id brightnessctl set +5% bindsym XF86MonBrightnessDown exec --no-startup-id brightnessctl set 5%- Note: keep one launcher only. People who bind dmenu on $mod+d and rofi on $mod+r end up searching two lists to find one app. Pick rofi (or pick nothing); one door is a desk, two doors is a puzzle. Warn: picom with experimental_backends = true was the classic tearing fix, but with vsync mis-set it becomes the tear cause. If frames stutter after enabling any compositor, the first suspect is its vsync: honest options are vsync = true (OpenGL) or no — not both worlds at once. 09 The fancy config, annotated Here is the target: one dark, gap-using, rofi-launched, notification-served i3 with iconed workspaces and a themed bar — every value explained by the comment on its line. This is meant to be read top to bottom ; every number is a real knob. # ~/.config/i3/config — the fancy build, annotated by line # --- identity ---------------------------------------------------------------- set $mod Mod4 # Super; swap to Mod1 if your desk prefers Alt set $term xterm # every exec below uses $term: change once set $menu rofi -show drun # theme lives in ~/.config/rofi/config.rasi font pango:JetBrainsMono Nerd Font 10 # the one font line the whole WM reads # --- the essential keys ------------------------------------------------------ bindsym $mod+Return exec $term bindsym $mod+d exec $menu bindsym $mod+Shift+q kill bindsym $mod+Shift+c reload bindsym $mod+Shift+r restart bindsym $mod+Shift+e exec "i3-nagbar -t warning -m 'You pressed exit shortcut. Do you really want to exit i3?' -B 'Yes, exit i3' 'i3-msg exit'" # --- focus, like arrows on tilers -------------------------------------------- bindsym $mod+j focus down bindsym $mod+k focus up bindsym $mod+h focus left bindsym $mod+l focus right # vim keys as well, free at the same bindings: bindsym $mod+Shift+j move down bindsym $mod+Shift+k move up bindsym $mod+Shift+h move left bindsym $mod+Shift+l move right # --- splits and layouts ------------------------------------------------------ bindsym $mod+b split h bindsym $mod+v split v bindsym $mod+f fullscreen toggle bindsym $mod+s layout stacking bindsym $mod+w layout tabbed bindsym $mod+e layout toggle split bindsym $mod+space focus mode_toggle # --- workspaces with glyphs, one block each ---------------------------------- set $ws1 "1: " # term set $ws2 "2: " # web set $ws3 "3: " # code set $ws4 "4: " # mail set $ws10 "10: " # settings bindsym $mod+1 workspace $ws1 bindsym $mod+2 workspace $ws2 bindsym $mod+3 workspace $ws3 bindsym $mod+4 workspace $ws4 bindsym $mod+0 workspace $ws10 bindsym $mod+Shift+1 move container to workspace $ws1 bindsym $mod+Shift+2 move container to workspace $ws2 # --- windows and rules ------------------------------------------------------- gaps inner 10 # i3 ≥ 4.24 (gaps merge) or i3-gaps: the breathing quantity gaps outer 4 smart_gaps on # no gaps when a single window fills the screen default_border pixel 2 # 1-2px: WM chrome you barely see but always find default_floating_border pixel 2 hide_edge_borders smart focus_follows_mouse no # focus by keys is a decision, not a hover accident Read it again with the annotations: nothing above is magic; it is all one concept per line . Introdução: A Necessidade de Mudança de Abordagem Contexto Operacional As forças de segurança e militares ao redor do mundo enfrentam um desafio crescente: a necessidade de intervir em situações complexas sem recorrer à força letal desnecessária. Tradicionalmente, a abordagem baseada puramente em táticas militares ou policiais convencionais tem resultadod em elevadas taxas de casualties entre civis, erosão da confiança das comunidades e, em muitos casos, consolidação do poder dos grupos criminosos que se fintem operadores legítimos. 1.1 A Falha dos Modelos Tradicionais O modelo tradicional de "identificar, perseguir, neutralizar" esbarra em limitações crucuais: Falha na Distinção: Não consegue diferenciar entre combatentes reais, cúmplices menores e civis envolvidos por circunstância; Erosão da Legitimidade: Quando a população sente que é alvo de operações militarizadas, coopera menos com as forças de segurança; Radicalização Secundária: Operadores desnecessários podem criar mais reclutas do que neutralizam; Questões Jurídicas: Ações desproporcionais violam o Direito Internacional Humanitário e convenções de direitos humanos. Alerta Operacional Desempenhar ações com a mesma lógica que os grupos criminosos — mesmo que com intenções distintas — não apenas é antiético como compromete a legitimidade institucional. Crime é Crime, independentemente de quem o comete. 2. Diferenciação: Inocentes vs. Culpados Este é o conceito fundamental que separa operações eficazes das que perpetuam violência cíclica. Não existe "colateral" quando se falha na diferenciação. 2.1 Arquitetura de Participação Todo grupo criminoso ou de perturbação possui uma estrutura hierárquica que pode ser mapeada: 👑 Nível 1: Líderes Estratégicos Tomam decisões de longo prazo, organizam logistics, estabelecem agendas políticas ou criminais. Este grupo é o principal alvo para desmantelamento. 🎯 Nível 2: Executores Diretos Realizam ações específicas sob ordens. Podem ser persuadidos a deserir ou cooperar com informações sobre os líderes. 🛡️ Nível 3: Cúmplices por Circunstância Fornecedores locais, informadores não conscientes, comunidade que tolera por medo ou necesidade económica. 🌱 Nível 4: Potenciais Recrutas Jovens ou marginalizados susceptíveis a serem recrutados. Intervenção precoce aqui previne expansão do grupo. 2.2 Indicadores de Distinção Matriz de Análise de Participação Indicador Participação Ativa Participação Passiva Nenhuma Participação Conhecimento Operacional Conhece planos, locais, rotas Sabe que algo ocorre, mas não detalhes Ignora totalmente Contribuição Económica Financia, fornece recursos diretamente Compra produtos de forma incidental Não interage com economia do grupo Apoio Logístico Hospeda, transporta intencionalmente Não oferece resistência, mas não ajuda Coopera com autoridades Motivação Ideologia, ganância, vingança ativa Medo, necessidade económica Neutralidade ou oposição Princípio Operacional Antes de qualquer intervenção, a questão fundamental deve ser: "Esta pessoa é essencial para a estrutura do grupo, ou é um elo que pode ser substituído sem comprometer as operações?" Se a resposta for "não essencial", o foco deve ser desengajamento, não eliminação. 3. Habilidades Psicológicas e Sociais para Análise Superior A capacidade de compreender comportamentos, motivos e estruturas sociais é tão crítica quanto qualquer tática de intervenção física. 3.1 Inteligência Social Operacional Desenvolver inteligência social não significa fingir ser amigo — significa compreender as dinâmicas reais das comunidades e grupos: Competências Essenciais Mapeamento de Redes Sociais: Identificar quem influencia quem, não apenas quem é o "chefe" aparente; Análise de Narrativas Locais: Compreender quais histórias, mitos e justificativas sustentam o grupo; Linguagem e Cultura: Falar a língua, compreender tabus e normas locais; Empatia Analítica: Entender por que alguém se juntou ao grupo sem racionalizar ou justificar a conduta; Detecção de Incongruências: Notar quando alguém age de forma inconsistente com seu papel declarado. 3.2 Técnicas de Persuasão e Desengajamento Muitas vezes, é possível desfazerrecrutar ou retirar suporte sem esforço físico: Oferta de Alternativas: Fornecer caminhos legítimos para quem participou por necessidade económica; Proteção ao Desengajar: Garantir segurança a quem decide cooperar ou abandonar o grupo; Quebra de Narrativa: Expôr contradições entre a retórica do grupo e sua realidade; Apoio Psicossocial: Trabalhar com comunidades para reduzir o apelo das narrativas extremistas. 4. Infiltration sem Apresentação como Police ou Militar Nota Ética Infiltration deve sempre ser feita dentro do quadro legal e ético, com supervisão adequada e com objetivos definidos. Nunca deve envolver o comprometimento de atividades ilegais ou a violação de direitos fundamentais. 4.1 Identidade Operacional vs. Identidade Investigadora A técnica de apresentar-se como similar ao grupo-alvo — sem ser police ou militar — baseia-se em: Interesses Comuns: Compartilhar interesses legítimos com o grupo (esporte, trabalho, community activities) sem aderir à sua ideologia; Observação Participativa: Participar de atividades periféricas para observar padrões sem ser identificado como investigador; Construção de Confiança Gradual: Estabelecer relações baseadas em interações recíprocas genuínas antes de coletar informações; Documentação Silenciosa: Registrar informações de forma não intrusiva, focando em padrões e anomalias. 4.2 O que Você Precisa Saber Conhecimento Essencial para Operadores Produtos e Serviços do Grupo: O que eles oferecem, como distribuem, quem compra; Cadeia de Comando Real: Não apenas quem está no topo, mas como as ordens fluem na prática; Interseções com Economia Legal: Pontos onde o grupo se conecta a sistemas financeiros legítimos; Patronagem Política: Se há apoio político, corporate ou estatal que sustenta o grupo; Fraquezas Internas: Conflitos internos, disputas por recursos, dissidência. 5. Identificação de Atividade: Técnicas de Análise 5.1 Coleta de Informação Passiva Antes de qualquer abordagem ativa, deve-se coletar o máximo de informação possível de forma não intrusiva: Fontes de Informação Open Source Intelligence (OSINT): Redes sociais, publicações, fóruns online, mídia local; Análise de Padrões de Tráfego: Fluxos de pessoas, veículos, mercadorias em rotas conhecidas; Análise Económica: Anomalias em transações, propriedades, gastos que não correspondem a fontes legítimas; Relatos da Comunidade: Informações de residentes, negócioss 증언os e organizações locais; Correlação com Dados Existentes: Cruzamento de registros policiais, fiscais, judiciais. 5.2 Técnicas de Análise para Melhor Precisão Desenvolver análise mais precisa requer: Análise de Redes: Mapear conexões entre indivíduos, locais, eventos; identificar nós centrais; Análise Temporal: Estudar padrões de atividade ao longo do tempo para identificar mudanças e tendências; Modelagem Preditiva: Usar dados históricos para identificar riscos futuros; Validação Cruzada: Confirmar informações com múltiplas fontes independentes; Análise de Impacto: Avaliar consequências de diferentes ações antes de implementá-las. Melhores Práticas Documente todas as fontes, métodos e raciocínios. Uma análise rastreável permite revisão, correção de erros e responsabilidade. Isso protege tanto os operadores quanto os cidadãos. 6. Exemplos Internacionais: Polícia e Military em Diferentes Países Para entender as diferenças de abordagem, examine como diferentes nações lidam com desafios de segurança: 6.1 Modelo Escandinavo (Suécia, Noruega, Dinamarca) Característica Abordagem Resultados Foco Prevenção, intervenção precoce, reintegração Baixas taxas de reincidência Uso da Força Último recurso, mínimo necessário Poucos feridos em operações civis Relação Comunitária Alta confiança, cooperação ativa Informação flui naturalmente Estrutura Polícia civilizada, mínimo militareização Percepção de legitimidade alta 6.2 Modelo de Segurança Comunitária (Colômbia pós-conflito) A Colômbia desenvolveu abordagens significativas para lidar com grupos armados sem recorrer a táticas puramente militarizadas: Guardianes de Comunidad: Membros da comunidade treinados para proteger suas próprias áreas sem constituir grupo armado; Justiça Restaurativa: Foco em reparação de danos em vez de apenas punição; Programas de Desmovilização: Oferecer alternativas reais para combatentes que desejam sair da luta. 6.3 Modelos de Militaryização Extrema Países que adotaram militarização completa da polícia frequentemente enfrentam: Escalada de Violência: Táticas letais levam a retalições; Perda de Inteligência: A comunidade para de cooperar; Custo Humano: Ferimentos e mortes entre civis não combatentes; Questões Jurídicas Internacionais: Violações do Direito Internacional podem levar a sanções e tribunais. Leitura Crítica O sucesso de diferentes modelos varia conforme o contexto histórico, cultural e político de cada nação. O que funciona em um ambiente pode falhar em outro. A crítica deve ser feita com base em evidências e não em generalizações. 6.4 Comparativo: Brasil, México e Espanha País Apostar Principal Desafios Documentados Leções Potenciais Brasil Polícia Militarizada em áreas urbanas Elevado número de mortes em confrontos, questionamentos sobre proporcionalidade Necessidade de differentiation entre trafficantes e civis México Operações contra cartéis com táticas militares Escalada do conflito, altos casualties, corrupção institucional Abordagem puramente militar não resolve causas estruturais Espanha Polícia cível com foco em inteligência Relativamente baixos casualties, alta cooperação comunitária Inteligncia e prevenção podem ser mais eficazes que força 7.
